title: Spot the Warning Signs of a Utility Scam
summary: Southern California Edison urges customers to be aware of scammers that threaten disconnection and demand immediate payment.
body_markdown:
The phone rings and the caller ID shows Southern California Edison. Someone posing as an SCE representative says your bill is past due and threatens to shut off your power and “freeze” your account unless you pay right now.


It’s a scam, and one that customers are reporting more often. For many, the reaction is panic, and scammers count on it.


To drive up the sense of urgency, they may even claim an SCE technician is just around the corner and can shut off your meter within minutes. Then they direct you to pay in a way that is hard to trace.


One of the most common fraudulent payment tactics is texting a barcode to your phone to use at a local retail store. There, you are asked to use the[code to send money](https://energized.edison.com/stories/beware-of-bogus-barcodes-and-websites) to the scammer and pay for your “outstanding bill”.


Because these payments often have transaction limits, scammers may have you repeat this action at several different retail locations, and the losses can add up quickly.


“Scammers pressure you to act without giving you time to confirm information,” said Peggy, an SCE information governance representative. “They tell customers to pay using nontraditional methods because it makes it harder to get your money back.”


These tactics reflect a broader[increase in utility scams](https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Scamiverse.pdf) . This year, customers have reported 1,880 scam incidents, a 31% increase from the same period in 2025.


Fraudsters have targeted both residential and business customers through phone calls, texts, emails and in-person visits. Through October, customers reported losing $176,453 to scams, surpassing the $131,464 in losses reported for all of 2025.


With scam incidents on the rise,[Utility Scam Awareness Day](https://www.utilitiesunited.org/) serves as a reminder to recognize the warning signs and stay vigilant.


The best advice is simple: Slow down and don’t let a scammer’s sense of urgency drive your decision.
